readerTitle: Same deal, two shops: why the bigger payoff isn't always the better bet
caseNote: 가상 사례 (주방용품 유통업체 두 곳, 운송 회사) + 일반적으로 관찰되는 현상 (위험한 대출자의 높은 금리, 주식과 국채의 장기 수익률 차이). 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 수익은 위험을 떠안은 대가다. 그래서 거래는 평균 수익이 아니라 '가장 나쁜 경우를 버틸 수 있는가'로 판단한다.
misconception: 평균적으로 더 많이 버는 쪽이 항상 더 좋은 선택이다. 위험을 더 지면 수익도 반드시 더 커진다.

sources.text: 재무관리의 표준 개념 (위험과 기대수익의 관계, 위험 프리미엄)
모든 거래 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 운송 계산: 비용 마일당 $1.90. 고정 $2.00 → +$0.10, 변동 평균 $2.30 → +$0.40, 최저 $1.70 → −$0.20. 운임 범위는 실제 시장 데이터가 아닌 가상 수치입니다.
'장기적으로 주식이 국채보다 수익률이 높았지만 변동도 컸다'는 일반적으로 받아들여지는 관찰입니다. 특정 수치나 기간은 일부러 쓰지 않았습니다. 게시 전 표현이 과하지 않은지 확인하세요.

cards.title: Same deal, two shops: why the bigger payoff isn't always the better bet
body: Two kitchenware distributors get the same offer from the same supplier. Same products, same prices, same odds.
One should say yes. The other should say no. Neither is making a mistake.

image.label: Two identical warehouses facing the same offer
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 거의 똑같은 두 창고가 나란히 서 있고, 가운데에 같은 계약서 한 장이 떠 있음. 왼쪽 창고 옆에는 큰 금고, 오른쪽 창고 옆에는 작은 돼지저금통. 실제 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: A sure $12,000 or a likely $15,000?
body: You distribute kitchenware. A supplier offers two deals for the holiday season.

**Deal A:** store and ship their stock for a flat fee of $12,000. **Deal B:** buy the stock outright for $60,000 and sell it yourself. A good season brings in $100,000. A bad one, and you clear it for $50,000. The odds look about even.

options.text: Deal A. A known $12,000 beats a gamble
options.feedback: You lock in your result and never lose sleep. The cost is the extra money a good season would have paid.

options.text: Deal B. It pays more on average
options.feedback: On average it does: $15,000 versus $12,000. But no business lives the average. You live one season, good or bad.

options.text: I'd need to know how much cash I have first
options.feedback: That's the question this lesson builds on. The deal is the same; what you can survive is not.

choice.afterReveal: Deal B earns more on average, but whether it's the better deal depends on whether you can absorb a $10,000 loss.

cards.title: Deal B's outcomes spread out.
body: Deal A gives one result. Deal B gives a range. Its average is higher, but so is the gap between best and worst: **$50,000**.

breakdown.label: Deal A, any season
breakdown.detail: Flat fee, no stock to sell

cards.title: Risk and return
body: **Return** is what you expect to earn. **Risk** is how far the real result can land from that expectation, especially on the downside.

The two usually travel together. A deal with a high return and no risk wouldn't last: everyone would rush in until the extra return disappeared. So higher expected returns tend to come with wider swings.

image.label: A narrow band of outcomes next to a wide one
image.brief: 두 개의 가로 띠 비교. 위쪽 'Deal A'는 $12,000 한 점에 좁게 모인 띠, 아래쪽 'Deal B'는 −$10,000부터 +$40,000까지 넓게 퍼진 띠이고 평균 $15,000 위치에 작은 표시. 음수 구간은 붉은색.

cards.title: Return is payment for carrying risk.
body: In Deal A, the supplier keeps the risk of unsold stock. So the supplier keeps most of the upside, and you get a smaller, safer fee. In Deal B, the risk moves to you, and so does the upside.

You see the same pattern everywhere. Lenders charge riskier borrowers higher interest. Over long periods, shares have generally earned more than government bonds, with much bigger swings along the way. **Whoever carries the risk expects to be paid for it.**

cards.title: Same deal, different answers.
body: Distributor one has $200,000 in the bank. A $10,000 loss is a bad month. Over many seasons, Deal B's higher average should win, so taking it makes sense.

Distributor two has $15,000 and payroll due in January. A bad season would leave it unable to pay staff. For this business, Deal B's average is irrelevant. **The question is not "what do I earn on average?" but "can I survive the bad case?"**

image.label: A $10,000 loss shown as small for one firm, huge for the other
image.brief: 같은 크기의 빨간 블록 '−$10,000'이 왼쪽에서는 큰 현금 더미 옆에 작게, 오른쪽에서는 작은 현금 더미를 거의 다 덮는 모습. 실제 로고 없음.

cards.softwareNote: A software founder faces the same trade: a fixed-fee custom project pays a known amount, while building a product for many users could pay far more or nothing. The deciding question is how many months the company can last if the product earns nothing.

cards.title: More risk doesn't promise more return.
body: Risk and return travel together in markets where people compete for good deals. That doesn't mean every risky bet pays well. Plenty of risky options have a *lower* average than the safe one. Those are just bad bets.
So check both sides. First, is the extra return real, or are you guessing the odds too kindly? Second, can you live with the worst realistic outcome?

cards.title: Now it's a trucking company.
body: Running your trucks costs about $1.90 a mile. A big shipper offers you a year of work, paid one of two ways: a fixed $2.00 a mile, or the market rate, which has averaged $2.30 but has dropped as low as $1.70.
You have about two months of cash in reserve. What do you choose?

options.feedback: You give up the higher average to stay alive through a bad stretch. With two months of cash, that's the trade worth making.

options.text: Market rate. It earns four times as much per mile on average
options.feedback: True on average: $0.40 versus $0.10 a mile. But at $1.70 you lose $0.20 on every mile, and a few slow months could empty your reserve.

options.text: Market rate now, and switch to fixed if prices fall
options.feedback: Flexible in theory. But fixed rates usually drop when the market does, so the safe option may cost more by the time you need it.

cards.title: Higher returns are payment for risk. Only take the risk you can survive.
body: Compare deals by their range of outcomes, not just their average. Then ask who carries the risk, and whether you'd still be standing in the bad case.
**Try it today:** pick one decision on your desk. Write down its best case, its worst case, and how many months of cash you'd have left after the worst.
